articles.title: Jayson Tatum vents over Jaylen Brown's 'cap' post as Celtics win overshadowed by trade drama talk
articles.text:
Jayson Tatum vents over Jaylen Brown's 'cap' post as Celtics win overshadowed by trade drama talk | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Boston Celtics' Jayson Tatum (0) grabs a rebound against New York Knicks' Karl-Anthony Towns (32) during the first half of an NBA basketball game, Friday, Oct. 23, 2026, in Boston. (AP Photo/Charles Krupa)
Jayson Tatum should have been breaking down the nuances of his 36-point performance in Celtics' 107-103 win over the defending champion New York Knicks.
Instead he spent most of his postgame news conference on Friday night addressing Jaylen Brown's social media response that took issue with Tatum saying in a video on his YouTube channel that he was “just as much caught off guard as the rest of the world” by Brown's trade to the Philadelphia 76ers this summer.
Brown responded on his Instagram account with a baseball cap emoji. “Cap” is slang for something that is not true. Asked if he had any response, Tatum sighed before expressing his frustrations with the entire situation for several minutes.
“I don’t have any animosity or beef, or ill will towards him. I think the toughest part is since he's not on the Celtics anymore, the narrative or the conversations haven't been enough about what we accomplished — all the games we won, winning a championship, how we've grown together. It's turned into this drama type of thing."
Tatum said while he understands there is an entertainment aspect to professional sports and that speculation about their off-court relationship is part of that, he was exasperated with how everything has lingered in recent months.
“I'm not blaming anybody for how they feel,” Tatum said. “We all go through different things in our lives. ... People play this game and never got the finals. We did it twice and won a championship. It should be more about that. This ain't no Shaq and Kobe. There's no beef.”
Both players have spoken glowingly at times about how they grew and thrived together during their nine years together as teammates.
But it's morphed into something else since the Celtics chose Tatum as the player they want to build around after trading Brown in what amounted to a move to cut one of the two players with $300 million contracts from the payroll.
“It’s turned into this drama type of thing,” Tatum said. "I've got two kids. I reached out the day he got traded. I called, I texted. And I understand, people process things differently. So, for me at this point in our lives, we are too old to be having our relationship discussed and X, Y and Z on the internet. There's a conversation to be had and we can definitely have that conversation. I welcome that, right?
“I've always wanted the best for him and wished the best for him. I've always publicly said those things.”
Tatum also lamented how social media has fueled it.
“I've seen all these things like, ‘Get your popcorn ready when they play.’ This ain't no (expletive) boxing match. Play basketball. There's no animosity. There's no beef. I just hate the way the conversation and narrative around it inflamed it. There's not enough communication. I think conversation would solve and put out a lot of fires."
Tatum also doesn't believe the conversation — if there is one — would be negative.
“He's just turned 30. I'm 28. I've got two kids. As adults, it's a conversation. I'm not saying it's a bad one or anything like that. Just communication usually gets to right (or) wrong, you'll understand the other side.”

articles.title: Brigham nurses reject contract deal, call for return to bargaining table
articles.text:
Brigham nurses reject contract deal, call for return to bargaining table | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Brigham And Women's Hospital, Boston. (Robin Lubbock/WBUR)
The unionized nurses at Brigham and Women’s Hospital have rejected a tentative contract deal — prolonging a bitter labor dispute and raising the possibility of another strike.
After two days of voting, the Massachusetts Nurses Association said the majority of its 4,000 members at the Brigham voted against the contract. Union officials did not immediately release the vote count.
Now, they say, they’ll ask hospital officials to return to the bargaining table within days.
After votes were counted Friday night, Kelly Morgan, chair of the bargaining committee, said hospital officials must work toward an agreement that recognizes “the value of Brigham nurses."
“This vote shows the resolve of Brigham nurses, who are fighting for patient safety and for the professional respect we deserve,” she said in a statement.
Hospital officials had presented the offer as their “last, best and final.” After nurses rejected it, they said the proposal "reflected the hospital’s commitment to investing in our nurses while supporting long-term sustainability," adding that it "kept Brigham nursing pay among the highest in the market."
“Although we are disappointed by the outcome, our priority and focus remain on providing safe, high-quality patient care,” they said.
Both sides had reached agreement on many provisions. But they were unable to compromise on wages.
Brigham nurses receive 5% increases every year for their first 20 years of service. The contract offer added 2.5% annual raises, for two years, for nurses at the top of the wage scale. But it lacked additional across-the-board increases that the union was seeking.
Union leaders argued they had a responsibility to allow the 4,000 members of their unit to vote on the deal — even while blasting hospital management for union busting.
“We have to remember that we are dealing with an employer who wants to eradicate us from their institution,” Morgan, a labor and delivery nurse, said in a recent social media post.
The union and the hospital — part of the Mass General Brigham health system — have been negotiating a new contract for a year. Mass General Brigham said it couldn't afford the pay increases that nurses initially demanded. This week the health system confirmed it was also cutting some jobs to save costs.
Tensions flared at the Brigham over the summer, and nurses staged a one-day strike in July. Hospital leaders locked them out for four more days while using temporary workers to care for patients.
Talks stagnated after the July strike, and the union scheduled a second walkout for Oct. 14. But instead of a one-day strike, they opted for an open-ended action that would continue until they got a deal.
That would have been disruptive for nurses — striking nurses don’t get paid — as well as for patients. Hospital leaders were gearing up to staff the Brigham with temporary workers again, and keep providing surgeries and other care while their staff nurses picketed outside.
The union postponed the strike after reaching a tentative agreement with hospital officials.
Union leaders still have the authority to schedule another strike — with 10 days’ notice. But they have not announced specific plans. After nurses rejected the hospital's contract offer Friday, they emphasized their goal is to return to negotiations.
The Brigham is one of the region’s busiest medical centers and represents the largest contingent of unionized nurses in the state. Senior nurses at the Brigham earn $220,000 a year, or more.
A couple miles away, Boston Medical Center and 2,000 nurses represented by a different union recently reached a deal that averted a potential three-day strike. That contract includes “meaningful” pay raises, especially for early-career nurses, according to the 1199SEIU United Healthcare Workers East.

articles.title: New England’s old buildings and old data centers could be upgraded to handle AI computing
articles.text:
New England’s old buildings and old data centers could be upgraded to handle AI computing | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
The data center in Trumbull, Conn. on Oct. 2, 2026. (Raquel C. Zaldívar/New England News Collaborative)
Right off the highway in Trumbull, Connecticut is a set of large, red brick buildings. They're a little bigger than a Walmart Supercenter, sitting on eight acres of land. This is the town’s data center.
It’s been around since the 1960s, and right now it’s in the middle of a major upgrade, one that will take it from regular computing to AI computing. Local residents, like Richard White, have some concerns.
“It could be a very large AI data center from a square footage point of view,” said White, who co-leads a group of concerned residents, known as the Trumbull AI Data Center Watch group.
“It’s currently small. We're okay with it remaining small, maybe, with the right regulatory environment. We don't want it to be bigger and we don't want more,” White said.
New England has dozens of small data centers like this, some of them decades old. With the increasing use of artificial intelligence, these facilities could get upgraded to handle AI computing. The changes can be hard to see from the outside and – for people who oppose them – even harder to stop.
Last month, Trumbull passed a two-year moratorium on new data centers, but that won’t stop its existing data center from being converted for AI.
The process is known as retrofitting. Instead of building a new data center from scratch, old buildings and data centers get renovated so they can handle the power and cooling needs of the computer chips that make AI work.
Trumbull town council representative for District 3, Jason Marsh (D), speaks during a town hall meeting on Sept. 9, 2026, in Trumbull, Conn. A moratorium on new data centers was passed during that meeting. (Ayannah Brown/Connecticut Public)
“The original data centers that we've had for years in our country use CPUs. These are the core computing chips that are in all of our laptops,” said Kenneth Gillingham, professor of environmental and energy economics at Yale School of the Environment.
AI computing relies on a different kind of chip, known as a GPU, that can process a lot more data. They use two to three times more energy and get hotter than the older chips.
“So what they will do is they'll pull out the old CPUs and they'll put in a whole bunch of the GPUs, and really fully swap what's actually in the data centers themselves,” Gillingham said.
Some AI in all data centers
Some AI experts say finding ways to make older data centers capable of running at least some AI is the way of the future.
“I believe strongly that we are going to see a very hybrid approach to data center design,” said Bill Kleyman, co-founder and CEO of Apolo.us, an AI company.
He says the types of things that small data centers do, like handling our emails or storing our photos, won’t go away, but those data centers could start doing more.
“I believe that in the very near future, we're going to have enough pressure from clients that a facility – let's say it's a 40 megawatt facility – is going to have to figure out a way to put AI infrastructure into their environment and either that or risk losing the customer,” he said.
If older data centers want to work with higher education, research institutions or financial organizations, they’re going to need to put in at least some AI equipment, Kleyman said.
Room for expansion
In Trumbull, First Selectman Vicki Tesoro said the AI upgrade won’t increase the existing data center’s size, water usage, electrical needs or generate more noise. But the property has a lot of room for expansion and locals are nervous about what happens if the data center grows in the future.
“There is a ton of potential on this property,” White said. “With the high-density AI racks that they talk about placing in this facility, they would run out of money and they would run out of power way before they run out of square footage.”
On Wednesday, Trumbull residents asked the town's planning and zoning commission to consider a 1-year-moratorium that would, in part, prevent current data centers from increasing in capacity or intensity. But the commission rejected the measure, stating the language in the moratorium was vague, making it difficult to enforce.
Connecticut Public requested a copy of 365 Data Centers’ letter of intent for the Trumbull site to learn more about the AI upgrades. A representative from the company denied the request, stating the document is confidential and non-binding and that there is no timeframe for future public announcements.
Earlier this month, White and other residents went on a tour of the data center with executives from 365 Data Centers and Aphorio Carter, the two companies leading the AI upgrade.
Talking face-to-face with the executives gave Trumbull resident Sherry Boyd a “tiny bit of piece of mind, like maybe 3%,” she said.
“But without having something official in writing where they can be held accountable for what they’re doing, we’re not going to let up until we have that,” she said.
Sarah Beck, who also lives in Trumbull, is less optimistic about the likelihood of the two companies sticking to their promises in the future.
Trumbull residents Sherry Boyd, left, and Sarah Beck, right, near a data center in Trumbull, Conn. on Oct. 2, 2026. (Raquel C. Zaldívar/New England News Collaborative)
“From my perspective, we’re not dealing with people. We’re dealing with a corporation,” she said.
“And then when they go back on their word, they’ll say ‘Tough cookies. You don’t have regulations in place. We never agreed to these things’. Those are the assumptions that I’m working under,” she said.
With White, Boyd and Beck lead the Trumbull AI Data Center Watch group. What they and others want is a written guarantee that the Trumbull data center will stay within the limitations they’ve set out and not turn into a giant AI data center.

articles.title: Buy your health insurance through the Mass. Connector? Open enrollment starts Friday
articles.text:
Buy your health insurance through the Mass. Connector? Open enrollment starts Friday | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Health Connector website. (Robin Lubbock/WBUR)
Massachusetts residents who buy health insurance through the  Massachusetts Health Connector can now make changes to their plans for a limited period of time.
Open enrollment on the state-run insurance marketplace began Friday and runs until Jan. 23, 2027. State and Boston officials said residents can take advantage of the Connector's assistance program, especially after recent federal changes to healthcare spending.
The Health Connector is a program for people who don't receive insurance from their job or make too much to qualify for MassHealth, the state's Medicaid program.
Dr. Bisola Ojikutu, Boston's Public Health Commissioner, said rising costs have made it more difficult for people to maintain their insurance, and that having health insurance is the "difference between life and death."
"Over the years, I have had patients living with HIV who've fallen out of care, patients living with diabetes who stopped their medication and literally ended up in the emergency department, and patients who delayed cancer screenings only to eventually present with late-stage disease," Ojikutu said Friday. "And that's all because of lapses in insurance coverage."
State officials urged residents who may be confused about coverage options to reach out to the Connector's Navigator program for assistance.
Boston officials said city residents concerned about buying health insurance can call the Mayor's Health Line.

articles.title: The Somerville Theatre's future is no longer in limbo
articles.text:
The Somerville Theatre's future is no longer in limbo | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Ian Judge, Jay O’Leary, Ian Brownell and Jamie Mattchen of CSB Theatres above the Somerville Theatre marquee. (Courtesy CSB Theatres)
Score one for the good guys. A team of employees and a loyal patron have purchased the Somerville Theatre building at 55 Davis Square, ending months of fraught speculation about the future of Greater Boston’s oldest and most beautiful movie palace. The sale secures the Somerville Theatre, the upstairs Crystal Ballroom and corner café Mr. Crêpe. They’ve also negotiated an extended 20-year lease on the Capitol Theatre in Arlington, easing the minds of local film buffs who panicked in July when both historic buildings were put on the market for $12 million each.
“It’s daunting,” admitted longtime Somerville Theatre manager and new co-owner Ian Judge, who will be celebrating his 25th year at the venue next May. “But we see this as a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to save these theaters for future generations. We've got great customer support, we've got great member support, so I feel like the trajectory is good. This is like a weird little miracle to me.”
The Somerville building is now owned by CSB Theatres, a group consisting of Judge and Capitol manager Jamie Mattchen, along with veteran employee Jay O’Leary and local film fixture Ian Brownell. (The initials stand for Capitol, Somerville and Ballroom.) CSB Theatres was formed in January of 2025, when members of the Fraiman family — who owned and operated both the Capitol and the Somerville for more than four decades — decided to get out of the movie business. CSB originally bought the leases and the liquor licenses to keep the theaters and the ballroom going. “We dreamed of buying the building someday, but that day came sooner than anticipated,” said Judge.
From left: Ian Judge, Jamie Mattchen, Jay O’Leary and Ian Brownell of CSB Theatres, the new owners of the Somerville Theatre building. (Courtesy CSB Theatres)
“It was like, oh s---, we have to do this now,” he laughed, speaking with Mattchen in the vestibule behind the Somerville Theatre’s balcony. The two were taking a much-needed break after seating a sold-out, opening night show of “ You Can See Everything.” You don’t often find business owners selling concessions and sweeping floors on Friday nights, but that’s how hands-on the CSB crew is. “We’ll get 800 people their popcorn, do this interview, then I’ll unclog a toilet and enter payroll,” said Mattchen, only half-kidding.
Obviously not in this for the glamour of show business, the two are passionate about keeping these neighborhood theaters alive for their communities. “Jamie lives in Arlington, I grew up three blocks from here,” Judge explained. His first job was as an usher at the historic Harvard Square Theater, which has been vacant on Church Street, collecting graffiti since 2012. “That's a perfect example of why you don't want somebody with resources but no imagination to buy a theater. Because how detrimental to Harvard Square is it to have that sitting there empty? This is where I live. This is where my family is from. If I had to drive through Davis Square and see that happening here, it would be a nightmare.”
Horror stories abound these days about the few remaining movie palaces being purchased and converted into god-awful “event spaces.” Exhibition aficionados still shed a tear over what’s become of San Francisco’s Castro Theatre or New York City’s legendary Ziegfeld. “What happened to the Castro 100% would have happened here,” said Judge. “It would certainly be the end of what is now a pretty reputable repertory house.”
Since Judge started working at the Somerville, he’s overseen its restoration from a dumpy, second-run discount theater into the jewel of Greater Boston cinemas. With its grand gold and red curtains that sweep back to unveil the 30-foot screen, sitting in the 840-seat main auditorium is like a return to Old Hollywood grandeur, except with a state-of-the-art projection and sound system capable of screening 35mm, 70mm and 4K digital presentations. The Somerville offers a mix of arthouse and blockbuster fare, along with repertory programming like their annual 70mm and Widescreen Festival, monthly “ Silents, Please!” screenings of classics with live musical accompaniment and their crowd-pleasing “ F**k the Nazis!” series, currently in its third depressingly necessary iteration. (Oh, and it’s also a music venue where U2 and Bruce Springsteen have performed. Not too shabby.)
Ian Judge onstage at the Somerville Theatre. (Courtesy CSB Theatres)
According to Judge, the down payment on the building was facilitated by “someone who wants to remain anonymous, who gave us money on very generous terms,” as well as CSB co-owner Ian Brownell, who’s something like the patron saint of the Boston film scene. In addition to his duties on the board of the Brattle Film Foundation and co-host of the Brattle Film Podcast, Brownell also founded the Screen Boston website and programs cool rep series for the Somerville from his extensive 35mm print collection. On the third Tuesday of every month, you can find him co-hosting the Crystal Ballroom’s monthly Movie Trivia Nights. “The Somerville Theatre has always belonged to the people who show up for it,” said Brownell. “Our names are on the paperwork, but the Somerville Theatre will always belong to its community.”
The CSB folks are confident that film fans will show up for the Somerville. They’ve started a GoFundMe to help pay down the immediate short-term debt, with a nonprofit arm to launch in 2027. “Normally you raise the money first and then you buy it, not the other way around,” laughed Mattchen, before getting serious. “We have almost never put our hands out and asked for help. This is the time when we need to, and it really counts.” She added that the announcement of the buildings being up for sale brought a much stronger response than they were

Boston Dynamics' Spot robot walks around during a demonstration at company's facility in Waltham in 2024. (Josh Reynolds/AP)
Dozens of Boston Dynamics employees are calling on the company to stop the sale of its AI-powered robot dogs to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Known as "Spot," Boston Dynamics' robots are dog-like autonomous machines with four legs that can climb stairs and do backflips. They're equipped with cameras and sensors.
The company faced some backlash in late August, when it was first revealed that the Department of Homeland Security planned to purchase the robots. A  $1.3 million contract with ICE was settled in September for the sale of four robot dogs and other Spot technology.
Employees wrote in a petition, obtained by WBUR and sent in early September to company leadership, that the sale hurts Boston Dynamics' image and "presents us as working directly with ICE" as the agency has "worked to sow fear" across the country.
A Boston Dynamics spokesperson confirmed the petition Friday, but said "nearly half" of its 300 signatures were entered as "Anonymous." The company employs more than 1,500 people.
"We cannot be proud of working at [Boston Dynamics] when that work is being used by a government agency that brutalizes civilians, including some of our own colleagues ... ," the petition read.
ICE previously said the robots would give them an additional safety tool that can "provide real-time situational awareness in hazardous, confined, or tactically uncertain environments" before agents are sent to a scene. The agency had added the robot dogs wouldn't replace "human judgment" from its law enforcement officers.
Boston Dynamics argues the dogs are being sold to ICE's Homeland Security Investigations unit, which primarily focuses on transnational criminal matters — not removal operations.
But Boston Dynamics employees said in the letter that the risk to the company is "too great to continue with this deal," adding it could cause staffers to quit or turn away potential new hires.
"Our public-facing teams have received external emails concerned about this deal," the petition read. "Many of us have gotten messages from friends and family, asking us in disbelief and horror if this news is true, and how we can live with ourselves if it is."
In a letter to employees, Boston Dynamics interim CEO Amanda McMaster wrote that after considering the petition, the company is standing by its decision to sell the robots to ICE.
McMaster said customers must comply with the company's terms and conditions for sale, which "prohibit any attempts to weaponize our robot or use it for purposes of harm or intimidation."
"I ask you to respect and accept this decision, even if you do not agree with it," McMaster wrote.
The company's  ethical principles state "if our products are being used for harm, we will take appropriate measures to mitigate that misuse." However, it's unclear what those mitigation measures would be.

articles.title: Counseling helps many students thrive. Is Conn. meeting the need on community college campuses?
articles.text:
Counseling helps many students thrive. Is Conn. meeting the need on community college campuses? | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Faculty advisor and professor Kelly O'Brien Mann facilitates a group discussion during the Healthy Minds Club at CT State Community College Tunxis in Farmington on Oct. 14, 2026. (Ryan Caron King/Connecticut Public)
On the Tunxis campus of Connecticut State Community College, a sign in front of a building reads, "Keep going. You’ve got this!"
Inside, some students quietly pore over books.
But in a more boisterous corner, with big windows facing some red-leaved trees, the Healthy Minds Club gathers in a classroom for its regular meeting. Faculty advisor Kelly O'Brien Mann talks to the group about the importance of setting goals in order to have a sense of purpose.
"If you don't know what is it you're working for, what's meaningful to you, what does your life look like in the future?" she asks.
The club's goal is to normalize talking about mental health. It’s a support group of sorts, where students share what they’re going through.
O'Brien Mann is a professor of psychology — but she wears more hats than that.
"In any given day, we might be doing counseling on the fly, and social work, and case management, and de-escalating, and helping students just problem solve with really complicated life issues," she said.
Across the country, studies show many students struggle with mental health. In a recent survey by the Healthy Minds Network, an organization that conducts research to help guide campus policies, about one third of U.S. college students reported symptoms of moderate or severe anxiety, and roughly the same share reported symptoms of moderate or severe depression.
At Tunxis, there are usually two wellness counselors on staff to provide mental health services. O’Brien Mann would like to see more counselors there, including a nurse practitioner for medication management.
Short-term counseling services on campus are free, though O'Brien Mann said students who have more chronic mental health conditions and need consistent counseling have to look outside CT State.
"Trying to find a therapist who has availability, who takes your insurance, is a tricky thing," O’Brien Mann said.
Kelly O'Brien Mann speaks with student Melanie Williams following a meeting of the Healthy Minds Club on Oct. 14, 2026. During the meeting, students shared issues they were working through and others chimed in with advice and assurance. (Ryan Caron King/Connecticut Public)
Other professors at Tunxis like Michael Hinton have concerns about crisis services being available.
"I'm walking this student down the hall trying to keep them calm and redirect them a little bit until we can get to mental health people," Hinton explained. "And I walk into a room just, fingers crossed, hoping that there's somebody here that can help."
'Mental health is a priority'
In Connecticut, mental health resources differ across state-funded schools. The University of Connecticut — the state's flagship four-year school — employs nearly three dozen mental health professionals, who serve about 32,400 undergraduate and graduate students across its campuses.
A UConn spokesperson said the school appointed a task force in 2020 to focus on students’ mental health needs, and it has expanded services and personnel.
CT State offers one to two counselors at each of its 12 community college campuses. The system enrolled almost 38,000 full- and part-time students in fall 2026, a spokesperson said.
Like UConn, the Connecticut State Colleges and Universities system has taken steps to enhance mental health services in recent years, including by joining JED Campus, a nationwide program of The Jed Foundation that helps schools evaluate and improve their support for students.
Nevertheless, this fall, CT State Tunxis started the semester with over 5,600 enrolled students and zero wellness counselors. The two counselors on campus left in the spring, and their positions weren't filled by the start of this school year.
O’Brien Mann said it's nobody's fault — it's just how things played out. But the lack of counselors speaks to a bigger problem for students in the community college system: an unmet need for more in-person mental health services.
"It would be great to say, 'Here are the names of the two counselors, here's how you get an appointment with them,'" O'Brien Mann said. "But I think understaffing for counseling has been a problem probably for every community college."
The open jobs at Tunxis are being filled, according to Meredith Yuhas, director of mental health and wellness at CT State Community College. Staffing challenges are not a new issue, she said.
"This is the situation that we've faced continuously," Yuhas said.
Yuhas said CT State is navigating a structural deficit and other financial pressures.
To help fill the gap for students, the college provides telehealth services with staff from a third-party contractor. The counseling and crisis support is free.
Yuhas acknowledged that having in-person counselors is important, and said the community college system is evaluating the needs on each campus.
"We have to be very intentional about staffing," Yuhas said. "I think everybody agrees mental health is a priority."
Ruth Pinto laughs as she talks with Eli Lund during the Healthy Minds Club meeting at CT State Community College Tunxis. (Ryan Caron King/Connecticut Public)
The mental health staffing at Tunxis has other people concerned, like psychology student Ruth Pinto.
Pinto helped a classmate get mental health support through the college’s CARE referral system, which connects students in distress with a multidisciplinary group of campus partners, such as faculty members, the accessibility and disability coordinator, the wellness counselor and the dean of students.
"All I wanted to do was the most important thing … to save his life and to save my friend who I love," Pinto said.
Pinto also became her friend’s health

articles.title: In last-minute reversal, Fields Corner Post Office will stay open
articles.text:
In last-minute reversal, Fields Corner Post Office will stay open | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
The Fields Corner Post Office located at 218 Adams Street in Dorchester. (Courtesy The Dorchester Reporter)
In an eleventh-hour reversal, the United States Postal Service (USPS) has secured a lease extension that will allow the Fields Corner Post Office to remain open at 218 Adams St., canceling a planned closure that was set to take effect on Monday.
The office was scheduled to close on Monday, Oct. 26.
Instead, postal customers can continue using the busy neighborhood branch without interruption, according to Boston City Councillor John FitzGerald.
FitzGerald shared a public notice generated by the USPS that announced the news.
“The Postal Service has secured a lease extension for the Fields Corner Post Office,” reads the public notice dated Oct. 23. “As a result, customers will continue to access postal products and services at 218 Adams St., Dorchester, MA 02122.”
Screenshot of USPS notice on Field Corner Post Office. (Courtesy The Dorchester Reporter)
The notice adds: “No action is required currently as there is no longer an imminent change to the location of this post office.”
The stunning about-face is welcome news for Fields Corner residents and business owners who had been bracing for the loss of a vital service.
Councillor FitzGerald confirmed the news to The Reporter on Friday morning.
“Through a great relationship with Senator Markey’s Office and a strong relationship with the developer and attorney at the O’Hearn Building, we were able to make sure parties connected and it worked,” said FitzGerald, who represents District 3, which includes the Fields Corner post office. “We’ve extremely happy with the outcome and Council President Breadon’s office for their help and all the residents that signed the petition and stepped up and fought for us.”
“This is what can happen when communities come together and fight for the services our neighborhoods depend on,” FitzGerald added.
The Postal Service had announced on Sept. 30 that the office would close temporarily on Oct. 26 because its lease was set to expire on Oct. 31. Under that plan, customers with post office boxes would have been redirected to the Fields Corner Carrier Annex at 18 Clayton St., while those seeking retail services would have been sent to the Codman Square Post Office at 554 Washington St.
A search for “alternate quarters” had been initiated to find another location, a spokesperson told the Reporter.
Friday’s announcement reverses that decision — at least for now. A long-term lease arrangement still needs to be finalized, FitzGerald said.
The threatened shutdown had prompted a wave of protests from elected officials and neighborhood residents, including Councillor FitzGerald, who launched an online petition urging postal officials to preserve a full-service branch in Fields Corner.
FitzGerald had also announced plans to seek support from his City Council colleagues through a formal resolution calling for the retention of postal services in the neighborhood.
The Fields Corner dispute also emerged amid a larger battle over the future of neighborhood post offices, particularly in Allston, where Mayor Michelle Wu, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley, and other elected officials have challenged the Postal Service’s efforts to permanently close a branch that has been shuttered since 2019.
The Fields Corner branch occupies space in the O’Hearn Building, a commercial property near the intersection of Adams Street and Dorchester Avenue. The building was sold last year and has been eyed for redevelopment, raising concerns about the long-term viability of the postal facility.
WBUR and the Dorchester Reporter have a partnership in which the news organizations share resources to collaborate on stories. This story was originally published by the Dorchester Reporter.
